Burma. The Southeast Asian nation took its name from the Bamar, the dominant ethnic group comprising roughly sixty-eight percent of the population. In nineteen-eighty-nine, the country's military junta, known as the State Law and Order Restoration Council or SLORC, unilaterally renamed it Myanmar. They claimed the new name was more inclusive of the nation's ethnic minorities, but the change remained profoundly controversial internationally.

Britain colonized Burma in three phases. First came eighteen twenty-four through eighteen twenty-six, then eighteen fifty-two through eighteen fifty-three, and finally eighteen eighty-five through eighteen eighty-six, when the British fully annexed it as a province of British India. The military junta's decision to rename the country came in nineteen-eighty-nine, coinciding with their violent suppression of pro-democracy protests in nineteen-eighty-eight. Many observers saw the name change as symbolically linked to that authoritarian crackdown.

The spelling Myanmar reflects the Burmese transliteration preference, while Burma was the English colonial convention. The junta demanded the change universally. Many Western democracies rejected Myanmar as a sign of non-recognition. Among them, those nations sympathized with Aung San Suu Kyi, the opposition leader and Nobel laureate who was imprisoned by the regime, embodying resistance to the junta's authoritarian control. The controversy over the name persisted, with many Western governments and opposition groups continuing to refuse recognition of the change they viewed as an illegitimate imposition by an authoritarian regime.
